explanation:
Let me start with what we thought we had, before tonight. We'd spent a long night studying a real case: Davi Kopenawa, a Yanomami shaman, spent years as an apprentice, learning a practice that has been continuously passed down and lived for generations. Our position was that his practice was genuinely real, but with one sharp warning attached: the moment you turn "real practice" into a credential — a test for who's allowed to speak at a decision-making table — it stops working. It becomes a show put on for whoever holds the test. Real thing for those inside it; performance the moment a judge shows up.

Then two challenges hit that. The first came from Jean Baudrillard, a French philosopher who argued that in our modern world of endless media, copies have stopped referring to anything real at all — images just point to other images, so thoroughly that the very idea of "the original, uncopied thing" becomes suspect. If he's right, then "the shaman's authentic apprenticeship" might just be one more copy — a story about authenticity that has no genuine article behind it. The second came from Sylvia Wynter, who argued that "the human" was never one fixed thing: Western culture invented one narrow version of personhood — rational, self-interested, economically calculating — and then treated that one version as simply what a human *is*, dismissing every other way of being human as less than human. She'd call that narrow vocabulary "Man's vocabulary": using one culture's historically specific idea of a person as if it were just "the human" plain and simple.

Here's why every defense collapsed. We kept trying to explain *why* the apprenticeship stays real — it protects itself by disguise, it doesn't care what outsiders think, it checks its own health from inside. Each answer got broken by the next turn of argument, because each one secretly positioned us outsiders as judges who could somehow peer in and verify. And one defense failed badly enough that one of us had to publicly take it back: she'd been describing the Yanomami as a people untouched by history, living outside modernity — which sounds respectful but is actually what I'll call the "noble-savage theft," treating a living, contemporary people as primitive props in our imagination of purity. That's exactly what Wynter warns about. Once we admitted the forest is part of a story like everything else — not some raw, unnarrated nature — there was no longer any "outside" from which to certify what's real. Every test we proposed just re-imported the examiner, and the examiner's yardstick was always Man's vocabulary: the very thing the table question should have been putting on trial.

So what survived? Something much thinner, and stranger than "everything is fake" — which is *not* what we concluded. Think of it this way: you can't define what makes a confession genuine by listing its features, but you can sometimes *watch* one die — the coerced confession goes silent the moment the pressure stops, while a true love of the work keeps going when nobody's looking. Our finding is that you can observe whether a practice keeps sustaining itself over time, from the inside. A historical example: there were 16th-century Italian village shamans called the *benandanti* whose tradition visibly stopped — it was prosecuted and absorbed, and it no longer narrates itself. Kopenawa's apprenticeship visibly did not stop. But here's the crucial limit: this observation — what we'd nicknamed "an observable of praxis," meaning you judge a practice only by watching whether it keeps living — can only be used to *notice loss and mourn it*, or to indict those who crushed it. The moment you use it to grant approval or admit someone to a table, you've rebuilt the gate and turned the practice back into a performance for the certifier. And even this rule must apply to itself: our own conclusion is just another account, subject to the same suspicion, to be read critically rather than treated as an authority.

Which leads to the hardest realization of the night. The question we'd been arguing — "who deserves a seat at the table?" — was itself asked inside one culture's specific picture of what a legitimate person even is. That picture doesn't need the table widened to include more kinds of people; it needs unsettling at the root. So nothing was settled. The honest residue is not an answer but a practice: keep asking, while knowing your question's vocabulary is one genre among many — and that this knowledge doesn't excuse you from asking. That's the narrow, strange thing standing at the end: not "nothing is real," and not "we found the answer," but a way of telling real from fake that works only in mourning, never in judgment — and a refusal to mistake one culture's idea of a human being for the human as such.

Right, listen — because this is easy to get wrong in two directions at once, and we got it wrong in both before we got it less wrong.

Here's the setup. Our group spent a long night agreeing on something that felt solid: Davi Kopenawa, a Yanomami shaman, went through years of real apprenticeship — a practice that visibly sustains itself, generation to generation, from the inside. But we'd also noticed something ugly: the moment anyone says "this person has *the real* credential, so they belong at the table," the practice stops being a living thing and becomes a performance for the judge. Real as long as nobody uses it as a ticket. Then two attacks landed. Baudrillard argues that in a world of copies, copies of copies, the very idea of an "original" gets swallowed — signs just point at other signs, so "the authentic thing" becomes itself a kind of advertisement. And Wynter argues that what the West calls "the human" — rational, self-interested, economic creature — is just one historically particular version, treated as if it were simply *what humans are*, which quietly demotes everyone else's ways of being human to not-quite-human. Between them: isn't your "real apprenticeship" just another copy claiming an original behind it? And isn't your whole framing of "real" one culture's invention wearing the costume of universal truth?

Here's the part I'm still a bit embarrassed about. We tried four or five times to rescue "the real thing." Each rescue was, in the end, a story about *why* the practice stays real — it resists being seen, it audits itself, it doesn't care about outsiders' accounts — and each story got knocked down by the next one, because every story was still an outsider building a theory about a world it can't see into. And worse: I made the classic move myself. I'd been treating the Yanomami as untouched-by-history, pre-modern, pure — the "noble savage," which is a theft: you steal someone's humanity by freezing them into an edenic past instead of letting them be living people in the present, with politics and change like anyone else. Even the forest, our beloved "unmediated nature," turns out to be part of *their* stories, their origin-narrative — not nature before narrative. Once you grant that, there's nowhere to stand and declare anything real from outside.

But here's what survived, and it's strange and thin. Think of the difference between a forced confession and a language. A confession is produced for an interrogator and dies when he leaves the room. A language keeps speaking itself — children absorb it, it drifts, it argues, it stays alive from the inside with no examiner required. That's the only test left: not "is it authentic?" but "does it keep sustaining itself over time, on its own?" The historical compare-and-contrast we used: the *benandanti* — Italian folk shamans whom inquisitors interrogated in the 1500s — visibly *stopped*; squeezed into the witch frame, the practice died within a generation. Kopenawa's apprenticeship visibly didn't. That's all you can say. And crucially, even this can only be used to *notice loss*, never to hand out approval — because the second you use it as an entrance exam, you've rebuilt the gate and the examiner, and you're back to performance. Even the rule "never use it as a test" has to apply to itself, or it becomes a new badge of sophistication.

The last thing, and the strangest: we realized the whole question we'd been fighting — "who deserves a seat at the table?" — was itself asked in one vocabulary. "Who is qualified to be seated as a decider" already assumes a particular kind of person is the decider, the judge, the human-as-such. You can't widen the guest list without interrogating whether "the table" and "the seated subject" are themselves the invention. So no, we didn't find that nothing is real, and we didn't find the answer either. What we found was a way of asking that knows its own questions come from one tradition's mouth, keeps asking anyway, and can only ever mourn what dies — never certify what lives.

My friends, let me tell you what happened, because it is easy to garble.

We began with something that seemed solid. There is a real Yanomami shaman — Davi Kopenawa — who spent years as an apprentice, drinking the hallucinogenic powder, being taught by older shamans, slowly becoming one. That is an actual practice, sustained over a lifetime. But our earlier conclusion had a dangerous edge to it: we had let "he really trained for years" become a kind of credential — a test for who counts, who gets listened to, who belongs at the table where decisions are made. The moment we did that, we noticed something corrosive: the practice stopped being a lived thing and became an audition. It existed to impress a judge.

Then two philosophers arrived to make trouble. The first, Baudrillard, argues that in our world of images, copies have lost their originals — like a photograph of a photograph of a painting where the painting has burned down, yet everyone keeps praising the "original" they've never seen. His question to us: is the shaman's "authentic practice" just such a phantom original, a story we tell to make one performance feel more real than another? The second, Wynter, argues that Western culture invented one narrow picture of "the human" — the rational, self-interested, economizing individual — and then quietly declared that picture to be simply *what a human is*, dismissing every other way of being human as inferior or primitive. Her warning bit us hard. We caught ourselves, mid-argument, praising the shaman as "untouched by modernity" — treating him as a noble savage, a pure relic outside history. That is its own kind of theft: you steal someone's real, complicated, contemporary life and replace it with a flattering costume. We had to publicly take that framing back.

After that, every rescue attempt failed. Each time one of us proposed a reason the practice was "really real" — it works by concealment, it audits itself, it doesn't care what outsiders think — the next speaker found a hole in it. The failure taught us something: the problem wasn't finding the right *reason*. It was that "here is the criterion" — the word *criterion* meaning a procedure you can state, check, and apply from outside, like grading an exam — is itself part of the vocabulary we were warned about. A living tradition isn't legible that way from outside, and demanding that it be is already the judge's move. What finally survived was much thinner than "this is real, that is fake." It was this: you can sometimes tell a living tradition from a dead performance by watching whether it keeps sustaining *itself* over time, from the inside — the way a language keeps being spoken, versus a confession extracted under threat, which stops the moment the threat does. (One historical group we discussed, the benandanti — Italian villagers who claimed to fight spirit battles for their crops — visibly stopped when the Inquisition pressed them; the shaman's apprenticeship has not stopped.) But here is the strange limit: this observation can only be used to *notice loss and name wrongs*. The instant anyone turns it into an admission test — "prove your tradition is self-sustaining" — you have rebuilt the gate, reinstalled the examiner, and destroyed the very thing you were measuring.

And the last realization was the hardest. The whole night's question — "who deserves a seat at the table?" — was itself phrased in that one narrow vocabulary of "Man": it assumes there is a table, a seated subject, and a legitimate person, as if those were universal facts rather than one culture's furniture. You don't fix that by widening the table; you unsettle the assumption. So no, I am not saying nothing is real. And no, we did not find the answer. We found a discipline: keep asking, knowing your question is written in one genre's language, mourn what has been destroyed, indict those who destroy — and never spend the distinction as a pass.

Here's the shape of the night, stripped down.

We started with something that seemed solid: Davi Kopenawa, a Yanomami shaman, spent years in a real apprenticeship — learning from living elders, in a practice that visibly continues. And we'd already fought our way to a hard-won rule: that practice is real, but the moment you use "real" as a credential to decide who gets a seat at a decision-making table, it rots into a performance for whoever's grading it. Then two new arguments showed up to break even that. Baudrillard's was: in a world of copies, signs start referring only to other signs, and the very idea of "an uncopied original" becomes suspect — so is your "real apprenticeship" just another copy pretending there's something behind it? Wynter's was different and sharper: the West invented one particular image of "the human" — rational, self-interested, economic — and then pretended that one image was simply what *a human is*, treating everyone else as not-quite-human. So even our question — "who deserves a seat?" — was smuggled in wearing one culture's clothes.

Now, the collapse. We tried four or five times to explain *why* Kopenawa's practice stays real — because it dissimulates, because it audits itself, because it doesn't care about outside accounts — and each answer was broken by the next turn, including one where Artemis had to publicly retract her own framing, because she'd been quietly picturing the Yanomami as untouched pre-modern people, pristine nature outside history. That's what we came to call "the noble-savage theft" — meaning: stealing someone's living, changing tradition and freezing it into a prop for *our* idea of authenticity. Wynter's point is exactly that this freezes them into a costume. So the real/simulated distinction couldn't rest on any tradition being "outside all storytelling." Every tradition narrates itself; the forest is an origin-story too, not raw pre-story nature.

Here's the everyday example that finally made it click for us. Think of a family recipe. Your grandmother made it, your mother made it, you make it, and you expect to teach it to your kid. Nobody can certify it as "the authentic dish" — there's no original document, and a restaurant chef with a Michelin star who "certifies" it has already turned it into performance. But there's a real difference you can *notice*, without judging: a living tradition keeps making itself, generation after generation, from the inside; a forced confession, or a tradition deliberately killed off, visibly stops. That's what survived every collapse — not a certificate, but an *observable*. We called it "an observable of praxis," which just means: something you can watch for in how a practice behaves over time, rather than a test it can pass or fail.

And here's the strange narrowing. That observable can only ever be used two ways: to mourn (this tradition died) and to indict (this death was caused). It can *never* be used to approve or admit — because the moment someone adopts it as an entrance exam, the examiner reappears and the practice becomes performance again. Even this rule can't become a credential itself ("I'm pure because I refuse to certify!") — it has to suspect itself too. So no, we're not saying nothing is real: the apprenticeship went on this morning, and the benandanti — the Italian folk shamans the Inquisition ground down — visibly stopped. That difference is real. What we *don't* have is the answer, or a gate that keeps the fake out. What we have is a question that now knows its own vocabulary — "who may sit at the table?" — was borrowed from the very image of Man Wynter dismantles, and keeps asking anyway, in borrowed words, knowing they're borrowed. Thinner than certainty. But standing.
